sources.title: AP Computer Science A Course and Exam Description (Effective Fall 2025)
AP Computer Science A Clarifications and Corrections to the Course and Exam Description
sources.revision: 2026-01-29 PDF revision (career-preparation wording implemented in August 2025; resource links and Progress Check edits announced for summer 2026; all 73 learning objectives unchanged)

mappings.summary: Design and express sequential everyday algorithms in plain prose or diagrams.
mappings.rationale: Graph lacks everyday algorithm design, sequencing, or flowchart/diagramming concepts; Algorithm Analysis measures asymptotic loop cost rather than introductory sequencing. Edge-only tuples also cannot express a standalone introductory topic without inventing an edge.

mappings.summary: Describe how source code is authored, checked by a compiler, and executed, including IDE support.
mappings.rationale: Graph contains no compiler, IDE, or source-to-execution lifecycle concepts, and standalone compilation concepts cannot be modeled in edge-only tuples without inventing edges.

mappings.summary: Distinguish compile-time syntax errors, logic errors found by testing, run-time failures, and exceptions.

disputes.rationale: Graph treats general Error Handling as a prerequisite, whereas AP CSA does not teach try/catch exception handlers and covers only specific runtime exceptions and throws IOException.

Graph requires Classes and Error Handling before Exceptions, whereas AP CSA introduces run-time exceptions in Topic 1.1 and arithmetic/bounds errors in Unit 1 before Unit 3 class creation, and omits general try/catch handling.

mappings.rationale: Graph includes Exceptions and Error Handling, partially touching runtime exceptions, but omits compile-time syntax errors and logic errors detected via testing.

mappings.summary: Choose between primitive and reference data-type categories for a stated problem requirement.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes References depend on Pointers, whereas AP CSA teaches Java object references without C-style pointers or address arithmetic (Pointers is outside the course).

mappings.rationale: Graph models Data Types and Objects separately, but links References to out-of-scope Pointers rather than Data Types and omits Java's primitive-versus-reference distinction.

mappings.summary: Declare typed primitive variables (int, double, boolean) to store numeric and truth values.
mappings.rationale: Variables and Data Types cover typed variable declarations generally, but the graph omits Java's three in-scope primitives (int, double, boolean) and the five excluded primitive types.

mappings.summary: Write and trace console output statements using System.out.print and System.out.println.
mappings.rationale: Program Input and Output broadly covers I/O operations without distinguishing Java console output or System.out.print versus System.out.println newline behavior.

mappings.summary: Construct and evaluate string literals including escape sequences for quotes, backslashes, and newlines.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Arrays before Strings, whereas AP CSA teaches String literals and methods in Unit 1 (and algorithms in Unit 2) before 1D arrays in Unit 4, without treating String as an array.

mappings.rationale: Graph includes Strings, but omits string literal syntax and escape sequences and places Arrays as a prerequisite before Strings.

mappings.summary: Write and evaluate int and double arithmetic expressions using +, -, *, /, %, precedence rules, and integer division by zero.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Classes and Error Handling before Exceptions, whereas AP CSA introduces run-time exceptions in Topic 1.1 and arithmetic/bounds errors in Unit 1 before Unit 3 class creation, and omits general try/catch handling.

mappings.rationale: Expressions and Data Types represent expression evaluation broadly, while Exceptions touches division errors, but Java int-versus-double truncation, modulo preconditions, precedence, and ArithmeticException are unmodeled.

mappings.summary: Initialize and update variables with = expressions, including null references, and trace stored values.
mappings.rationale: Variables and Expressions reflect state and evaluated expressions generally, but omit = assignment semantics, uninitialized-variable rules, and null references.

mappings.summary: Write Java code that reads input supplied to a program.
mappings.rationale: Program Input and Output identifies the general input topic, with no evidence of how to write Java code to read input. The course excludes any particular input form as a requirement (CED p. 35).

mappings.summary: Apply explicit (int) and (double) casts and implicit widening in arithmetic, including truncation and rounding patterns.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no primitive type-casting, widening, truncation, or floating-point rounding concepts.

mappings.summary: Identify integer overflow when 32-bit int calculations exceed Integer.MIN_VALUE through Integer.MAX_VALUE.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no fixed-width 32-bit integer bounds or overflow concepts (Integer.MIN_VALUE / Integer.MAX_VALUE).

mappings.summary: Explain floating-point round-off errors caused by finite double representation precision.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no floating-point precision limit or double round-off error concepts.

mappings.summary: Write and trace compound assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=) and postfix ++ and -- variable updates.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=) or postfix increment/decrement concepts.

mappings.summary: Read library and API documentation to determine a class's data attributes, methods, and package grouping.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.

mappings.rationale: Classes, Objects, and Encapsulation reflect class attributes and behaviors generally, but Java API specifications, packages, and library lookup are absent.

mappings.summary: Document code behavior, preconditions, and postconditions with line, block, and Javadoc comments ignored by the compiler.
mappings.rationale: Graph omits source code comments, Javadoc generation, preconditions, and postconditions, and edge-only tuples cannot represent a standalone documentation topic without inventing an edge.

mappings.summary: Select the matching method to invoke from documentation and method parameter signatures.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Functions depend on Control Flow, whereas AP CSA teaches method signatures and calling library/instance methods in Unit 1 prior to branching and loop control flow in Unit 2.

mappings.rationale: Functions reflects callable procedures with variables, but omits Java method signatures, parameter ordering, and procedural abstraction from API docs while placing Control Flow ahead of Functions.

mappings.summary: Explain method invocation rules for void and non-void methods, call-by-value arguments, overloading, and control flow return.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Functions depend on Control Flow, whereas AP CSA teaches method signatures and calling library/instance methods in Unit 1 prior to branching and loop control flow in Unit 2.

mappings.rationale: Functions reflects procedural calls generally, but omits void versus non-void return rules, call-by-value copies, and method overloading, and disputes Control Flow ordering.

mappings.summary: Invoke static class methods with the class name and dot operator and trace their return values.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no concept of static class methods or invoking methods on a class identifier rather than an instance.

mappings.summary: Write and evaluate expressions calling Math.abs, Math.pow, Math.sqrt, and scaled Math.random ranges.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no java.lang.Math library methods or scaled Math.random range generation concepts.

mappings.summary: Explain classes as object blueprints, Object as Java's universal superclass, and conceptual superclass/subclass relationships without designing hierarchies.

disputes.rationale: Graph includes taxonomic edge Abstract Classes is_a Classes; runtime traverses is_a identically to depends_on, yet Abstract Classes is outside Fall 2025 AP CSA and taxonomy does not prove an instructional prerequisite.
Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.
Graph connects Inheritance to Classes; Fall 2025 AP CSA 1.12.A.2 explicitly excludes designing and implementing inheritance hierarchies while keeping only conceptual awareness of Object.

mappings.rationale: Classes and Objects touch instance-versus-blueprint concepts, but the graph omits Object as root class, disputes Classes depending on Objects, connects out-of-scope Inheritance, and attaches taxonomic edge Abstract Classes is_a Classes.

mappings.summary: Declare variables of reference types that hold references to objects.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes References depend on Pointers, whereas AP CSA teaches Java object references without C-style pointers or address arithmetic (Pointers is outside the course).

mappings.rationale: Objects, References, and Variables cover reference variable declarations broadly, but References depends on out-of-scope Pointers.

mappings.summary: Match a constructor call to its signature among potentially overloaded constructors.
mappings.rationale: Graph contains no constructor, constructor signature, or constructor overloading concepts.

mappings.summary: Declare reference variables typed for objects or initialized to null.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes References depend on Pointers, whereas AP CSA teaches Java object references without C-style pointers or address arithmetic (Pointers is outside the course).

mappings.rationale: Variables, Objects, and References touch object-reference declarations, but omit null initialization and depend on out-of-scope Pointers.

mappings.summary: Instantiate objects with new, passing constructor arguments by value and tracing constructor execution.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.

mappings.rationale: Classes and Objects touch object types, but constructor invocation with new, call-by-value constructor parameters, and constructor control transfer are absent.

mappings.summary: Invoke instance methods on object references with the dot operator, trace outcomes, and recognize NullPointerException on null targets.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.

Graph requires Classes and Error Handling before Exceptions, whereas AP CSA introduces run-time exceptions in Topic 1.1 and arithmetic/bounds errors in Unit 1 before Unit 3 class creation, and omits general try/catch handling.
Graph makes Functions depend on Control Flow, whereas AP CSA teaches method signatures and calling library/instance methods in Unit 1 prior to branching and loop control flow in Unit 2.

mappings.rationale: Objects, Classes, Functions, and Exceptions relate to method calls on objects, but Java dot-operator dispatch and NullPointerException are missing and prerequisite ordering is disputed.

mappings.summary: Create immutable String objects, concatenate strings with primitive or toString values, and trace results.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Arrays before Strings, whereas AP CSA teaches String literals and methods in Unit 1 (and algorithms in Unit 2) before 1D arrays in Unit 4, without treating String as an array.

mappings.rationale: Strings and Objects exist in the graph, but String immutability, java.lang defaults, primitive concatenation, and implicit toString are absent and Strings depends on Arrays.

mappings.summary: Invoke String methods (length, substring, indexOf, equals, compareTo) and recognize out-of-bounds index exceptions.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Arrays before Strings, whereas AP CSA teaches String literals and methods in Unit 1 (and algorithms in Unit 2) before 1D arrays in Unit 4, without treating String as an array.

mappings.rationale: Strings and Exceptions partially relate to string operations and index bounds errors, but Java Quick Reference String methods (length, substring, indexOf, equals, compareTo) are absent and Strings depends on Arrays.

mappings.summary: Express everyday algorithms combining sequence, conditional choice, and repetition in prose or diagrams.
mappings.rationale: Control Flow, Loops, and Iteration cover selection and repetition concepts, but omit representing everyday algorithms in prose or diagrams.

mappings.summary: Write and evaluate Boolean expressions that compare primitive values or reference identity with == and !=, and test numeric ordering with <, >, <=, and >=.
mappings.rationale: Boolean Logic and Expressions provide a general basis for Boolean comparisons. The graph gives no evidence for numeric ordering or the distinction between comparing primitive values and reference identity.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace one-way if and two-way if-else branching statements.
mappings.rationale: Broad Control Flow combines all branching constructs without explicitly distinguishing one-way if and two-way if-else selection.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace nested if and multiway if-else-if selection chains.
mappings.rationale: Broad Control Flow does not distinguish nested if branches or multiway if-else-if selection order.

mappings.summary: Construct and trace compound Boolean logic with !, &&, and ||, operator precedence, and short-circuit evaluation.
mappings.rationale: Broad Boolean Logic does not distinguish compound logical operators (!, &&, ||), precedence, or short-circuit evaluation from simple Boolean expressions.

mappings.summary: Prove Boolean equivalence using truth tables and De Morgan's laws.

disputes.rationale: Discrete Mathematics depends on Sets (outside AP CSA), so truth-table and De Morgan equivalence cannot rely on Discrete Mathematics as verified course evidence.

mappings.rationale: Boolean Logic depends on Expressions, which supports the idea of comparing logical expressions. Truth tables and De Morgan's laws are missing. The upstream Sets dependency is outside course scope.

mappings.summary: Compare object references for alias identity (==, !=, null) versus attribute equality (equals).

disputes.rationale: Graph makes References depend on Pointers, whereas AP CSA teaches Java object references without C-style pointers or address arithmetic (Pointers is outside the course).

mappings.rationale: Objects, References, and Boolean Logic relate to object comparison, but == alias checks versus .equals() equivalence and null checks are unmodeled and References depends on Pointers.

mappings.summary: Recognize problems needing iteration and diagnose zero-iteration conditions, infinite loops, and off-by-one bugs.
mappings.rationale: Loops and Iteration cover repetition broadly, but omit zero-iteration guards, infinite-loop conditions, and off-by-one error analysis.

mappings.summary: Write and trace while loop repetition governed by a pre-checked Boolean condition.
mappings.rationale: Generic Loops and Iteration nodes do not distinguish pre-test while loops from counted or enhanced loops.

mappings.summary: Write and trace for loops with header initialization, guard, and update, and convert between for and while.
mappings.rationale: Generic Loops and Iteration nodes do not model for-loop header initialization/guard/update phases or for-to-while equivalence.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace standard non-collection algorithms for divisibility, integer digits, counts, min/max, and sums or averages.
mappings.rationale: Control Flow, Loops, and Iteration cover underlying mechanisms without specifying standard non-collection algorithms (divisibility, digit extraction, min/max, sums/averages).

mappings.summary: Implement and trace iterative algorithms that search, count substrings, and reverse strings.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Arrays before Strings, whereas AP CSA teaches String literals and methods in Unit 1 (and algorithms in Unit 2) before 1D arrays in Unit 4, without treating String as an array.

mappings.rationale: Loops, Iteration, and Strings cover components of string iteration, but standard substring search/count/reversal algorithms are unmodeled and Strings depends on Arrays.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace nested loops where the inner loop finishes completely on each outer iteration.
mappings.rationale: Loops and Iteration do not distinguish nested loop execution where inner loops run to completion on each outer step.

mappings.summary: Trace loops to count statement executions and compare iterative run-time efficiency informally.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Discrete Mathematics (and Sets) before Algorithm Analysis, pulling formal proofs out of scope for Unit 2 informal execution counting.

mappings.rationale: Algorithm Analysis touches run-time counting, but AP CSA 2.12.A uses informal statement execution counts without formal Discrete Mathematics or asymptotic complexity.

mappings.summary: Plan class-based programs in prose or diagrams specifying data attributes, procedural decomposition, and method behaviors.

disputes.rationale: Graph includes taxonomic edge Abstract Classes is_a Classes; runtime traverses is_a identically to depends_on, yet Abstract Classes is outside Fall 2025 AP CSA and taxonomy does not prove an instructional prerequisite.
Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.

mappings.rationale: Classes, Composition, Encapsulation, and Functions support parts of class abstraction, but prose/diagram design, static versus instance attributes, and method decomposition are unmodeled.

mappings.summary: Analyze software reliability, beneficial and harmful societal, economic, and cultural impacts, and open-source versus proprietary licensing.
mappings.rationale: Unit Testing depends on Functions, which relates to checking behavior under varied conditions for reliability (CED 3.2.A.1). This tuple leaves social and economic effects, ethical trade-offs, and software licensing unaddressed.

mappings.summary: Apply public and private access modifiers to classes, instance fields, constructors, and methods to enforce encapsulation.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.

mappings.rationale: Encapsulation covers information hiding in classes, but omits Java public/private rules for top-level classes, constructors, instance variables, and helper methods.

mappings.summary: Declare private instance fields, initialize object state in constructors (copying mutable arguments), and apply default constructor rules.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.

mappings.rationale: Classes, Composition (has-a), and Variables cover instance attributes conceptually, but omit constructors, mutable parameter copying, and Java default field values.

mappings.summary: Author void mutators and typed non-void accessor or computation methods using primitive parameters passed by value and return flow.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.
Graph makes Functions depend on Control Flow, whereas AP CSA teaches method signatures and calling library/instance methods in Unit 1 prior to branching and loop control flow in Unit 2.

mappings.rationale: Classes and Functions touch methods with variables, but omit accessor/mutator conventions, void versus non-void class methods, and Java primitive pass-by-value rules.

mappings.summary: Write and trace methods taking and returning object references, observing aliasing, mutable state effects, and same-class private access.

disputes.rationale: Graph makes Classes strictly depend on Objects; while Unit 1 introduces using library objects before Unit 3 class creation, AP CSA 1.12.A defines an object as an instance of a class blueprint.
Graph makes References depend on Pointers, whereas AP CSA teaches Java object references without C-style pointers or address arithmetic (Pointers is outside the course).

mappings.rationale: Objects, References, Classes, and Functions touch object references, but omit parameter aliasing, returning object references, and same-class private access, while References depends on Pointers.

mappings.summary: Write static class methods that operate on static state and class helpers without direct instance state access.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no concept of static class methods or restrictions on accessing instance state without an object parameter.

mappings.summary: Declare shared static class variables and final constants with appropriate visibility.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no concept of shared static class variables or final constants.

mappings.summary: Determine variable visibility across blocks, constructors, methods, and parameters, including local shadowing of instance fields.
mappings.rationale: Scope models lexical visibility within Functions, but omits block-level scope, constructor parameter scope, and shadowing of class instance variables.

mappings.summary: Use this within instance methods and constructors to refer to or pass the active receiver object (unavailable in static methods).
mappings.rationale: Graph has no self-referencing this keyword concept or distinction between instance and static contexts.

mappings.summary: Explain personal privacy hazards from collecting and retaining user data and a developer's responsibility to safeguard privacy.
mappings.rationale: Graph lacks personal data privacy risk concepts, and an isolated ethics/privacy topic cannot be represented in edge-only tuples without inventing an edge.

mappings.summary: Identify risks from algorithmic bias, biased collection practices, and incomplete or inaccurate data sets.
mappings.rationale: Graph lacks algorithmic bias, data quality, and incomplete/inaccurate dataset concepts, which cannot be encoded standalone without inventing edges.

mappings.summary: Evaluate whether a data set is fit to answer a specific problem without invalid extrapolation.
mappings.rationale: Graph lacks dataset fitness and extrapolation scope judgment concepts.

mappings.summary: Represent everyday data-set workflows and tabular or charted structures in prose or diagrams prior to coding.
mappings.rationale: Graph lacks everyday data-set representation via charts, tables, and diagrams.

mappings.summary: Create fixed-size 1D primitive or object arrays via new or initializer lists, index with [], check .length, and handle bounds errors.
mappings.rationale: Arrays covers 1D array concepts and Exceptions touches bounds failures, but fixed .length, default element values, initializer lists, and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException are omitted.

mappings.summary: Traverse 1D arrays with indexed for/while loops and enhanced for loops, distinguishing element-variable copies from object state updates.
mappings.rationale: Arrays, Loops, and Iteration cover array traversal mechanisms, but omit Java enhanced for loop variable-copy versus mutable-element semantics.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace 1D array algorithms for extrema, totals, quantifiers, counts, adjacent pairs, duplicates, shifts or rotations, and reversal.
mappings.rationale: Arrays, Loops, and Iteration support general array iteration without specifying standard algorithms (consecutive pairs, duplicates, shifts, rotations, reversal).

mappings.summary: Read persistent text files using java.io.File, Scanner, throws IOException, hasNext/next methods, literal String.split, and close.

Graph requires Arrays before Strings, whereas AP CSA teaches String literals and methods in Unit 1 (and algorithms in Unit 2) before 1D arrays in Unit 4, without treating String as an array.

mappings.rationale: File Handling covers reading persistent files, but omits Java File, Scanner, throws IOException, and literal String.split, while pulling in disputed Error Handling and Strings->Arrays edges.

mappings.summary: Use immutable Integer and Double wrappers with their primitives through boxing and unboxing. Use parseInt and parseDouble to parse strings into primitive numbers.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no Integer/Double wrapper classes, autoboxing, unboxing, or parseInt/parseDouble concepts.

mappings.summary: Create parameterized ArrayList<E> collections from java.util and trace size, add, get, set, and remove.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Polymorphism (and Inheritance) before Generics, whereas AP CSA uses ArrayList<E> without teaching polymorphism or inheritance.

mappings.summary: Traverse ArrayList collections safely, handling index shifts on deletion, IndexOutOfBoundsException, and ConcurrentModificationException.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no ArrayList traversal, deletion index-shift, or ConcurrentModificationException concepts.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace ArrayList manipulation algorithms (including insertion and deletion) and parallel multi-collection traversals.
mappings.rationale: Graph has no ArrayList insertion/deletion algorithms or simultaneous multi-collection traversal concepts.

mappings.summary: Represent rectangular 2D arrays as arrays of row arrays, index via [row][col], inspect row and column lengths, and handle bounds errors.
mappings.rationale: Graph models only 1D Arrays and graph-specific Adjacency Matrices, omitting rectangular 2D arrays of arrays, [row][col] access, and row/column length attributes.

mappings.summary: Traverse 2D arrays in row-major, column-major, or custom orders using nested indexed or enhanced for loops.
mappings.rationale: Graph omits 2D array representation and row-major versus column-major nested traversal semantics.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace 2D array algorithms across full grids, specific rows or columns, or subsections.
mappings.rationale: Graph omits 2D array grid, row, column, and subsection algorithms.

mappings.summary: Implement and trace linear search across 1D arrays, ArrayList instances, and row-by-row 2D arrays.
mappings.rationale: Linear Search covers sequential search on 1D structures, but omits searching ArrayList collections and row-by-row linear search in 2D arrays.

mappings.summary: Trace each pass of iterative selection sort and insertion sort on arrays and ArrayList collections.
mappings.rationale: Graph covers Insertion Sort on Arrays, but completely omits Selection Sort and ArrayList sorting.

mappings.summary: Trace recursive methods with base cases, per-call local variables, and iterative equivalence without authoring recursive code.
mappings.rationale: Recursion covers recursive function invocation and Iteration supports equivalence, but base cases, per-call stack frame isolation, and AP CSA's exclusion of writing recursive code are omitted.

mappings.summary: Trace recursive traversals over strings, arrays, and ArrayList collections.

disputes.rationale: Graph requires Arrays before Strings, whereas AP CSA teaches String literals and methods in Unit 1 (and algorithms in Unit 2) before 1D arrays in Unit 4, without treating String as an array.

mappings.rationale: Recursion depends on Functions, and Strings and Arrays supply two data types for recursive traversal. The graph omits ArrayList and leaves the Strings-to-Arrays ordering disputed.

mappings.summary: Trace each step of iterative or recursive binary search on sorted collections and compare efficiency to linear search.
mappings.rationale: Binary Search covers recursive binary search on sorted Arrays and Linear Search exists, but iterative binary search, ArrayList search, and an efficiency comparison link between Binary Search and Linear Search are absent.

mappings.summary: Trace recursive divide-and-merge steps of merge sort on arrays and ArrayList collections.
mappings.rationale: Merge Sort covers recursive divide-and-merge sorting on Arrays, but omits ArrayList sorting required alongside arrays in AP CSA 4.17.C.

outside_course.reason: Unit 4 collection objectives use 1D and 2D arrays and ArrayList. AVL tree balancing requires a separate tree representation and rotations.

Unit 3 covers writing concrete Java classes and methods. The Abstract Classes is_a Classes tuple describes a subtype relationship, and abstract class design falls beyond those class-creation objectives.
Unit 4 traverses arrays and ArrayList. Adjacency lists encode neighbors for graph algorithms, a separate use of collections.
Objectives 4.11.A–4.13.A use 2D arrays for indexing and traversal. Adjacency matrices additionally encode graph connectivity.
Topic 4.17 uses recursion for data traversal, binary search, and merge sort. Backtracking adds exploration and reversal of candidate choices.
